blocks.text: Have you ever wondered how algorithms efficiently handle large datasets? The secret often lies in the divide-and-conquer approach, which breaks problems into smaller, manageable pieces.

blocks.markdown: Divide-and-conquer is a powerful algorithmic paradigm that involves breaking a problem into subproblems, solving each subproblem independently, and combining their solutions to solve the original problem. This unit explores classic algorithms that utilize this approach, including binary search, merge sort, the closest pair problem, and fast integer multiplication.

blocks.title: Divide-and-Conquer
blocks.text: Divide-and-conquer is an algorithm design paradigm that recursively breaks down a problem into two or more subproblems of the same or related type, until these become simple enough to be solved directly. The solutions to the subproblems are then combined to give a solution to the original problem.

blocks.markdown:
### Binary Search
Binary search is a classic example of a divide-and-conquer algorithm. It efficiently finds the position of a target value within a sorted array by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half.

blocks.title: Binary Search Example
blocks.prompt: Find the index of the number 23 in the sorted array [3, 9, 15, 23, 42, 56, 78] using binary search.

steps.text: Start with the entire array. Set the low index to 0 and the high index to 6.
Compare the middle element (23) with the target (23). They are equal.
The target is found at index 3.

blocks.answer: The number 23 is found at index 3.

blocks.markdown:
### Merge Sort
Merge sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that divides the array into halves, recursively sorts each half, and then merges the sorted halves to produce the sorted array.

blocks.title: Merge Sort Complexity
blocks.text: Merge sort has a time complexity of \( O(n \log n) \) for both the best and worst cases, making it one of the most efficient sorting algorithms.

blocks.title: Merge Sort Example
blocks.prompt: Sort the array [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10] using merge sort.

steps.text: Divide the array into two halves: [38, 27, 43, 3] and [9, 82, 10].
Recursively divide [38, 27, 43, 3] into [38, 27] and [43, 3], and [9, 82, 10] into [9, 82] and [10].
Merge the final two sorted arrays: [3, 9, 10, 27, 38, 43, 82].

blocks.markdown:
### Closest Pair Problem
The closest pair problem involves finding the pair of points that are closest to each other in a set of points on a plane. A divide-and-conquer approach can solve this problem more efficiently than the brute force method.

blocks.markdown:
### Karatsuba Multiplication
Karatsuba multiplication is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that multiplies two numbers faster than the traditional method. It reduces the multiplication of two \( n \)-digit numbers to at most \( n^{\log_2 3} \approx n^{1.585} \) single-digit multiplications.

blocks.title: Karatsuba Multiplication Example
blocks.text: To multiply two 4-digit numbers, Karatsuba's algorithm divides each number into two 2-digit numbers, performs three multiplications, and combines the results using addition and subtraction.

points: Divide-and-conquer algorithms break problems into smaller subproblems.
Binary search and merge sort are classic examples of divide-and-conquer.
Karatsuba multiplication is more efficient than the traditional method for large numbers.
